explain.title: What biomolecules are
explain.body: The molecules produced by organisms are called biomolecules or biological molecules. They include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). They are mostly large in size and are called macromolecules.

explain.title: Where they are found and what they do
explain.body: Biomolecules occur in different cell locations and have different roles. Carbohydrates provide and store energy; proteins can act as enzymes, form structures, and control cellular traffic; lipids store energy, insulate against heat, and form part of cell membranes. DNA carries genetic information, while RNA carries information from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

explain.title: Biomolecules in dry mass
explain.body: Biomolecules make 93% of the dry mass of protoplasm. The remaining 7% comprises vitamins and inorganic substances. Of the listed biomolecules, proteins make up 50%, nucleic acids 18%, carbohydrates 15%, and lipids 10%.

explain.title: Metabolism
explain.body: All the chemical reactions that occur in an organism are collectively called metabolism. Anabolism combines simpler substances to form complex substances and uses energy. Catabolism breaks complex molecules down into simpler ones and releases energy.

explain.title: Biochemistry and molecular biology
explain.body: Biochemistry is the study of the chemical processes that occur within living organisms. Molecular biology is the study of the structure and function of the biomolecules.

mistakes: Do not confuse anabolism with catabolism: anabolism builds complex substances, while catabolism breaks them down.
Do not say that anabolism releases energy; it uses energy, whereas catabolism releases energy.
Do not mix up the dry-mass percentages: proteins are 50%, nucleic acids 18%, carbohydrates 15%, and lipids 10%.
Do not confuse the role of DNA with that of RNA: DNA carries genetic information, while RNA carries information from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis.

explain.title: Carbohydrates and their classes
explain.body: “Carbohydrate” means ‘hydrated carbons’. They are the organic compounds in which the ratio of H and O is 2:1 (same as in water). They are also known as “Saccharides” (meaning sugar). They have the general formula Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ where n is the number of carbon atoms. There are three classes of carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.

explain.title: Monosaccharides
explain.body: Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are made of single sugar molecule. They are easily soluble in water and have sweet taste. They may have 3 to 7 carbon atoms. Pentoses (5 C) and hexoses (6 C) are most common. Ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses; glucose, fructose, and galactose are hexoses.

explain.title: Disaccharides and polysaccharides
explain.body: Disaccharides are made of two monosaccharides units. They are less soluble in water and are less sweet in taste. Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose; maltose is made of two glucose molecules. Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharides units. They are insoluble in water and are tasteless. Examples include starch, glycogen, cellulose, and chitin.

explain.title: Sources and functions
explain.body: Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy. Glucose is used by cells to produce energy through cellular respiration. Dietary fibre contains indigestible carbohydrates e.g., cellulose. It helps for the proper bowel movements. Ribose and deoxyribose are essential parts of RNA and DNA respectively. Plants convert monosaccharides to disaccharides like sucrose for transport. Cellulose supports plant cells and ultimately the whole plant.

mistakes: Do not confuse sucrose with maltose: sucrose is glucose plus fructose, while maltose is two glucose molecules.
Do not call starch a disaccharide; it is a polysaccharide.
Do not say all carbohydrates are sweet or soluble: polysaccharides are tasteless and insoluble in water.
When giving a role for cellulose, distinguish its structural support in plants from its role as dietary fibre in bowel movements.
Do not mix up plant starch and animal glycogen: starch is stored in plants, while glycogen is mainly stored in the liver and muscles.

explain.title: DNA has a double helix structure

notes.title: Biomolecules and metabolism
notes.answer: Biomolecules are molecules produced by organisms. Metabolism is the total of the chemical reactions in an organism.
notes.explanation: Biomolecules are molecules made by organisms. They help build cells and carry out life processes. Metabolism includes all the chemical reactions in an organism: anabolism builds complex substances, while catabolism breaks them down.
notes.simple: Cells contain different kinds of large molecules. Some provide or store energy, some build cell structures, and some carry genetic information. The chemical reactions happening in an organism are called metabolism.
examples: Proteins make up 50% of the dry mass of protoplasm.
Anabolism combines simpler substances to form complex substances.
steps: Remember the four main groups: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
Use the table to connect each biomolecule with its location and function.

notes.title: The three classes of carbohydrates
notes.answer: A disaccharide is made of two monosaccharide units.
notes.explanation: Carbohydrates are grouped by how many sugar units they contain. Monosaccharides have one unit, disaccharides have two, and polysaccharides have hundreds to thousands. Their taste and solubility also differ.
notes.simple: Think of sugar units like building blocks: one block is a monosaccharide, two joined blocks are a disaccharide, and a very long chain is a polysaccharide.
examples: Glucose is a monosaccharide; sucrose is a disaccharide.
Starch is a polysaccharide found in plants.
steps: Look for how many sugar units the carbohydrate contains.
One unit means monosaccharide; two units mean disaccharide; a very large number means polysaccharide.
Use taste and solubility as extra clues: monosaccharides are sweet and easily soluble, disaccharides are less sweet and less soluble, and polysaccharides are tasteless and insoluble.

notes.title: Proteins: building blocks and jobs
notes.answer: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Their functions include forming cell structures, catalysing biochemical reactions, regulating body processes, transporting oxygen, enabling muscle contraction, clotting blood and defending against pathogens.
notes.explanation: Proteins are polymers made from amino acids. Amino acids have a central carbon attached to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and an R group. The R group differs between amino acids. Proteins have many roles, including building structures, catalysing reactions, transporting oxygen and defending the body.
notes.simple: Proteins are like long chains made from amino-acid units. The different amino acids and their order help make different proteins with different jobs.
examples: Glycine has H as its side group.
Alanine has CH₃ as its side group.
steps: Identify the amino acid units as the building blocks of proteins.
Remember that the R group varies between amino acids.
Link a protein to its function: for example, haemoglobin transports oxygen.
Use examples from the text to support your answer.

notes.title: Lipids: fats, oils and membranes
notes.answer: Lipids include fats, oils and phospholipids. Fats and oils contain glycerol and three fatty acids; phospholipids contain glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group.
notes.explanation: Lipids do not dissolve in water, but they dissolve in some organic solvents. Many lipids are made from glycerol and fatty acids. Fats usually contain saturated fatty acids and are solid at room temperature; oils contain unsaturated fatty acids and are liquid at room temperature. For example, animal fats are usually solid, while olive oil is liquid.
notes.simple: Think of glycerol as a small backbone. Fatty acids attach to it to make many lipids. The type of fatty acid helps determine whether a fat is solid or an oil is liquid at room temperature.
examples: Animal fats are examples of fats containing saturated fatty acids.
Olive oil is an example of an oil containing unsaturated fatty acids.
steps: Remember that glycerol has three carbon atoms, each with a hydroxyl group.
A fatty acid has a long hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl group (COOH) at the end.
Identify saturated fatty acids by their carbon-to-carbon single bonds; they are solid at room temperature.
Identify unsaturated fatty acids by one or more carbon-to-carbon double bonds; they are liquid at room temperature.

notes.title: Nucleic Acids: DNA and RNA
notes.answer: Nucleic acids are made of nucleotides. DNA carries hereditary information, and RNA helps with protein synthesis.
notes.explanation: Nucleic acids are built from nucleotides. DNA stores hereditary information, while different types of RNA help use that information to make proteins.
notes.simple: Think of DNA as information written in a sequence of bases. RNA helps carry and use that information so a protein can be made.
examples: A nucleotide contains a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group.

steps: A nucleotide has a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group.

notes.title: How DNA instructions make a protein
notes.answer: DNA → mRNA by transcription; mRNA → protein at a ribosome by translation.
notes.explanation: A gene is a sequence of DNA nucleotides that carries information for making a specific protein. The sequence is copied into mRNA by transcription. The mRNA goes to a ribosome, where its sequence is used to join amino acids into a protein. This is translation.
notes.simple: DNA keeps the instructions. A copy of the instructions travels to a ribosome, which uses them to make a protein.
examples: mRNA → amino acids joined into a protein at a ribosome: translation.
steps: A gene is a specific sequence of DNA nucleotides that carries information for making a specific protein.
The DNA sequence is copied into messenger RNA (mRNA). This is transcription.
The mRNA carries its nucleotide sequence to a ribosome.
The ribosome reads the mRNA sequence and joins specific amino acids to make a protein. This is translation.

notes.answer: Biomolecules are molecules in living things, including carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

Water is the medium in which many of these processes occur.
notes.simple: Living things contain different kinds of molecules. Each kind has a particular job, such as providing energy, building structures, or carrying instructions.

steps: Carbohydrates include sugars and starches; they are a major energy source.

modelAnswer: Water is a good solvent, so many biomolecules and ions dissolve in it.

It helps maintain suitable conditions, including temperature, for biomolecules to work.
Therefore, without water, many biomolecular reactions and life processes could not function properly.
